pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Communication with Light & Sound ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4] communicate over a distance)

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum — KS1 Design & Technology, bridged):** At age 6–7 England has not yet taught the light/sound SCIENCE (Light is Year 3, Sound is Year 4), so this task is anchored in KS1 Design & Technology: pupils 'design purposeful, functional, appealing products'; 'generate, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing and templates'; 'select from and use a range of tools and materials'; and 'evaluate their ideas and products against design criteria'. The underlying science of why light/sound carries the signal comes later — stated honestly.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 1-PS4-4, engineering-integrated):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]." (Clarification: examples [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4]. Assessment boundary: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4].) Cross-linked to the K–2 engineering-design PEs — K-2-ETS1-1 (define the problem), K-2-ETS1-2 (sketch/model a solution), K-2-ETS1-3 (test and compare two designs) — and DCI PS4.C (people use devices to send and receive information over long distances).

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL engineering-design task, so the learning is the DESIGN–BUILD–TEST–IMPROVE cycle, not an explanation of the physics (respect the assessment boundary). Open with a defined, relatable problem — 'send a message to a friend across the room / who is too far to hear you' — then have children plan/sketch a device, build it from real tools and materials (cup-and-string telephone for sound; a torch signaller for light; a drum for a beat pattern), and TEST whether the message actually gets across the distance, then improve it. Crucially, agree a simple shared CODE (one flash = yes, a drum pattern = a message) so the device transmits real INFORMATION, not just noise or light — communication is information transfer, not merely output. Normalise redesign: the string must be pulled taut, the signal must be seen/heard and understood at the far end. Integrate simple distance measurement (how far can the message still be received?) and compare two devices' strengths and weaknesses.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, hands-on procedural). Mastery = the child defines the communication problem, designs and builds a working device, tests it over a real distance and improves it, and can say how it uses light or sound to send an agreed message — without needing to explain the underlying physics (deferred to Y3/Y4 science and later).
bestPractices: Open with a defined, relatable problem ('send a message to a friend across the room / who can't hear you') per K-2-ETS1-1, so the build has a real purpose.
Run the FULL iterative cycle — define → sketch/plan → build → test over a real distance → improve — and normalise redesign rather than expecting a one-shot product.

Provide real tools and materials and let children physically make the device (cup-and-string telephone, torch signaller, drum); keep focus on whether the signal gets across, not on explaining the physics (assessment boundary).
Have children sketch or model their design to communicate it before/while building (K-2-ETS1-2).
Agree a simple shared CODE (one flash = yes; a drum pattern = a message) so the device carries real information — communication is information transfer, not just making light or noise.
Test and compare: measure how far the message still carries, and weigh two devices' strengths and weaknesses (K-2-ETS1-3, integrating simple 1.MD measurement).
Connect to real communication technologies (telephone, lighthouse, drums, semaphore) so children see that devices carry information over distance (DCI PS4.C).
keyRepresentations: The design–build–test–improve loop shown as an iterative cycle (define → plan → build → test → improve).
Cup-and-string telephone (sound) and torch/flashlight signaller (light) as the two canonical build options.
A simple agreed code/key (a flash pattern or drumbeat = an agreed message) — the information the device carries.
A distance-measured test track — how far away can the message still be received clearly?
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the device just needs to make light or sound, rather than carry an AGREED message over the distance — communication is information transfer, not mere output.
Treating design as one-shot ('I built it, I'm done') instead of an iterative test-and-improve process.
Believing a string telephone works best SLACK — in fact the string must be taut to carry the vibration; a loose string kills the signal.
Assuming a louder or brighter device is automatically 'better', rather than testing whether the message actually gets across clearly at the far end.
Confusing 'communicating' with just making a noise or shining a light at someone — with no shared code, no information is sent.

learn.summary: For 6–7 year-olds, teach communication with light or sound as a design-build-test-improve engineering task: the child defines a real problem (send a message to a friend across a distance who can't hear them), plans and physically builds a device (cup-and-string telephone for sound, a torch signaller for light, or a drum for a beat pattern), agrees a shared CODE with the receiver so the device carries real information, then tests it over a measured distance and improves it. The big idea is that communication is information transfer — not merely making light or noise. The underlying physics (why light or sound carries the signal) is deferred to later years and need not be explained here.

activities.title: Build and test a real signal device over a distance
feedback: If the receiver cannot say what the message meant, point back to the code: 'How did your friend know what your flashes MEANT — what did you agree before you started?'

When a cup-and-string telephone fails, check the string: it must be pulled taut and kept from touching anything to carry the vibration well; a loose string, or one touching something, weakens the sound so much that it may not be heard.

If a message is misunderstood, help the child diagnose before reacting: 'Was the problem what your flash MEANT, or that your friend couldn't see it at all?' A wrong meaning needs the agreed code fixed; a flash genuinely too dim to be seen (or a gap too wide) can legitimately be improved by more brightness or a shorter distance. Judge success at the receiving end — does the message arrive and get decoded correctly — rather than just by how bright or loud the signal is.
After a first failure, prompt the cycle rather than the physics: 'It didn't work the first time — what did you change, and why did that help?'
Success is when the friend correctly receives the intended message, not simply when a light or sound was produced.
activities.rationale: The standard's learning lives in the tactile making and the iterative redesign: defining the problem, sketching a solution, building with real tools, testing over a real distance, and improving. Keeping focus on whether the message arrives (not on explaining the physics) respects the age-appropriate boundary that light and sound science comes in later years.

1-PS4-4 is engineering-integrated and cross-links to the K–2 engineering-design PEs: K-2-ETS1-1 (define a simple problem), K-2-ETS1-2 (develop a simple sketch/drawing/physical model), K-2-ETS1-3 (analyse data from tests of two objects to compare strengths and weaknesses). The design process is iterative (define → design/build → test → improve), not linear. DCI PS4.C: people use a variety of devices to communicate over long distances.
learnerActions: Name the problem out loud: 'I need to send a message to a friend who is across the room and can't hear me speak.'
Sketch or describe a plan for a device before building it — choose light (a torch signaller), or sound (a cup-and-string telephone or a drum beat pattern).
Build the device from real tools and materials.
Agree a simple shared code with your partner BEFORE sending, e.g. one flash = 'yes', two flashes = 'no', or a drumbeat pattern for an agreed word.
Send the message and check with your partner whether they received the intended meaning correctly.

If it fails, work out WHY before changing something: if the meaning was wrong, fix or clarify the agreed code; if the signal could not be seen or heard at all (e.g. a slack string, or a flash too dim across a wide, bright room), pull the string taut, make the flash brighter, or shorten the gap.
Measure how far apart you can stand and still have the message arrive correctly.
Build or test a second device and compare the two: which carries the message further, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of each?
activities.intendedInsight: A device communicates only when an agreed code AND a well-built device work together to carry a real message over the distance — communication is sending information, not just producing light or noise.

activities.title: Define and brainstorm the problem with an inventor
feedback: If the child proposes only 'make a light' or 'make a noise', push on meaning: 'How will your friend know what it means?'
Reward ideas that name both a device AND an agreed code.

Treat this as a planning primer — the ideas here should be built and tested for real afterwards; the dialogue can prompt the define/brainstorm phase but does not itself produce a built, tested device.
activities.rationale: A spoken, in-role dialogue genuinely suits the DEFINE and BRAINSTORM phases at the front of the design process, prompting children to articulate the problem and the idea of a code before building. It is a design-thinking primer and should hand off to a physical build rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: 1-PS4-4 is engineering-integrated and cross-links to the K–2 engineering-design PEs: K-2-ETS1-1 (define a simple problem), K-2-ETS1-2 (develop a simple sketch/drawing/physical model), K-2-ETS1-3 (analyse data from tests of two objects to compare strengths and weaknesses). The design process is iterative (define → design/build → test → improve), not linear. DCI PS4.C: people use a variety of devices to communicate over long distances.
learnerActions: Take on a real scenario: an inventor needs to signal a ship at sea, or send a message to a friend across a valley.
Answer the inventor's questions: What problem are we solving? Who needs to receive the message, and why can't we just walk over or shout?
Brainstorm ways light or sound could carry the message — flashes, drumbeats, a string line between two cups.
Answer the pushback: 'How will they know what your flash MEANS?' — propose a code.
Hand off your best idea to the building stage and actually make it.
activities.intendedInsight: Good design starts by clearly defining the problem and the audience, and by planning how the signal will carry a meaning — not just how to make a signal.

activities.title: Explore real communication devices and their codes
feedback: Prompt children to name the code each device uses, not just what it looks like.
Connect each example back to the child's own build: 'Which of these gives you an idea for sending your message?'
Use this as idea-priming background; it shows examples but has no build-and-test loop, so it supports rather than replaces the hands-on making task.
activities.rationale: Seeing real communication technologies supports the background idea that people use devices to send information over distance (DCI PS4.C) and sparks design ideas. It has no build-and-test loop, so it supports but does not replace the hands-on design task.
sourceClaims: 1-PS4-4 is engineering-integrated and cross-links to the K–2 engineering-design PEs: K-2-ETS1-1 (define a simple problem), K-2-ETS1-2 (develop a simple sketch/drawing/physical model), K-2-ETS1-3 (analyse data from tests of two objects to compare strengths and weaknesses). The design process is iterative (define → design/build → test → improve), not linear. DCI PS4.C: people use a variety of devices to communicate over long distances.
learnerActions: Look at real communication devices one at a time: cup-and-string telephone, lighthouse, drum, semaphore flags, bell.
For each, work out how it sends a signal far away and what 'code' it uses — flashes, beats, flag positions, rings.
Play a 'what message is this sending?' guessing game for a given signal.
Use the examples to spark ideas for your own device and code.
activities.intendedInsight: People across history use many different devices to send information over distance, and each relies on an agreed code — giving ideas for your own design.

activities.title: Quick check on design steps and signal types
feedback: Confirm that a string telephone works with a TAUT string; a slack string does not carry the vibration.
If the design steps are ordered wrong, re-run the sequence pointing back to the last build the child actually did, and note that after 'improve' you often loop back to test again.

Treat this as a light knowledge check: it can confirm recognition of the step order and light-vs-sound sorting, but it does not elicit the independent construction of a working device, so it supplements rather than replaces building and testing.
activities.rationale: A short ordering/sorting check can confirm adjacent knowledge (step order, light-vs-sound, taut-string fact), but it assesses recognition and cannot produce the working device the standard requires, so it supplements rather than carries the design-build task.

learnerActions: Put the design steps in order: define → plan → build → test → improve.
Sort devices into 'uses light' versus 'uses sound'.
Answer: 'What makes a string telephone work — a taut string or a slack string?' (Correct answer: taut.)
activities.intendedInsight: The design process has a usual working order and is iterative (you loop back to improve), and different devices rely on light or on sound to carry a signal.

constraints: The deepest version of this learning is an actual physical build with real tools and materials, tested over a real distance — hands-on making, the taut-string fix, and iterative redesign are central to the standard's verb 'design and build'.
Keep focus on whether the signal and its meaning get across; do not require children to explain the underlying physics of why light or sound carries the signal (deferred to later years).
Agreeing a shared code in advance is essential: without it, producing light or noise transmits no information and the task is not complete.
Normalise redesign — the first attempt is expected to need improvement; do not treat design as one-shot.

Judge success by whether the receiver decodes the intended message correctly over the distance, not by how bright or loud the signal is. Note that a genuinely too-dim or too-distant signal can still be a legitimate thing to improve; the point is that brightness/loudness alone is not the measure of successful communication.

A screen-based signal activity can rehearse the define-design-build-test-improve loop and the encode-a-message-over-distance idea, but it is a rehearsal of the design thinking, not the physical build the standard calls for; use it as a fallback or supplement, not a replacement.
Spoken brainstorming and device-example exploration support only the define/brainstorm and idea-priming phases and must hand off to a real build.
Recognition checks (ordering steps, sorting light vs sound) assess adjacent knowledge and do not elicit independent construction of a working device.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three source claims were marked unverified in the original row (the K–2 engineering-design cross-links and the England DfE curriculum placement); treat their specifics as unconfirmed.

The original material in places implied a screen/2D model was the 'best available' vehicle only because a true physical maker option was absent (a noted catalog gap); this rewrite restores the physical build as the primary activity and treats on-screen versions as fallbacks.

Corrected a potential learner error carried from the original: 'louder/brighter' is NOT a general fix for a misunderstood message — when meaning fails to arrive, the fix is usually the agreed code or clarity; however, a genuinely too-dim or too-distant signal can legitimately be improved by brightness or a shorter gap. The actions, feedback and constraint now distinguish these cases in learner-facing text, not only here.

Claims that a static image 'cannot teach' the design loop, or that 3D 'adds nothing', were softened to scoped statements about what each medium does and does not rehearse; no comparative efficacy is asserted beyond the source claims.

The NGSS 1-PS4-4 build-requirement claim is attached to the recognition-check rationale because it establishes the build the check cannot satisfy; whether this counts as direct support is borderline and noted in the preservation audit.

probeDeeper: How did your friend know what your flashes MEANT — what did you agree before you started?
It didn't work the first time — what did you change, and why did that help?
Would shouting or flashing brighter have fixed it, or was it something about the code?
assess.correctAnswer: The child designs a device/method AND agrees a shared CODE with the partner (e.g. one flash = yes, two = no; or taps for letters), keeps a cup-string phone TAUT, sends the message, checks whether the partner decodes it correctly, and — if it fails — diagnoses why and changes something before retrying. Success = the friend correctly receives the intended message.

errorPatterns.pattern: Communication = just making a signal: flashes the torch or makes a noise with no agreed meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Information transfer needs a shared code agreed in advance; judge success by whether the message arrives, not by whether a light or sound was produced.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sends signals without first agreeing what they mean; the partner can't decode the message

errorPatterns.pattern: One-shot design: treats the first attempt as finished, with no testing or improving
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the design cycle — test, find the fault, change one thing, retry; design is iterative, not one-shot. Don't reteach light/sound, just prompt the cycle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds once and stops; doesn't test or iterate even when it fails

errorPatterns.pattern: Slack string / brighter-is-better: leaves the string slack, or 'fixes' a failed message by just being louder or brighter
errorPatterns.nextMove: A cup-string phone needs a TAUT string to carry the vibrations; if the message comes through wrong, it's the CODE or clarity to fix, not the loudness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects a slack string to carry the message, or responds to a decoding failure by increasing volume/brightness rather than fixing the code

responseLevels.gap: Produces light/sound with no agreed code, or stops after one attempt; the message doesn't arrive and isn't diagnosed.
responseLevels.full: Designs a method with an agreed code, keeps the device working (taut string / clear signal), tests whether the partner decodes the intended message, and iterates on failure by changing something specific — explaining how the light or sound carried the information.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees a basic code and sends a message, but doesn't check whether it arrived correctly, or doesn't improve the design when it fails.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your job: send a short secret message to a friend across the room without speaking or walking over. Using a torch (or a cup-and-string phone), design a way to do it, agree with your friend how it works, then send the message and see if they get it right. If it doesn't work, change something and try again.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is watched, not asked about. A child who grasps communication sets up an AGREED code and tests whether the message actually ARRIVES (is decoded correctly), then iterates on failure. A child who doesn't just makes light or noise with no shared code, calls it done after one try, or thinks brighter/louder is the fix. The give-away is whether they check that the friend understood.
